newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - Potential new UK liabilities.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - Potential new UK liabilities.

text.p: Insurers of UK casualty risks are concerned about two potential developments this year which could significantly add to higher-level exposures.

The first stems from the British National Health Service (NHS), which currently has lawyers looking at whether it could become able to recover the cost of healthcare from third party insurers of parties held responsible for the accident which puts a victim into an NHS hospital.
This is part of a world-wide trend by which governments are increasingly seeking to off-load the cost of the mushrooming social security bill from taxpayers to somebody else.
As reinsurance broker Willis Faber & Dumas (WF&D) warns in a recent market bulletin, insurers are the natural target to be that "somebody else".

With a UK general election looming, such moves might be cynically described as using the insurance market to raise taxes for the government by describing them as insurance premiums. It is, after all, the policyholder who pays in the end. The effect could be to increase significantly the cost of awards, magnify larger claims and thus impact the reinsurance market as well.

The second area of concern is a move to scrap the civil litigation rule book used in High courts and County Courts and replace it with a radical new procedural system. This could affect both the way responsibility is laid and the size of awards given, both of which would have an impact on UK liability insurance. The proposals, drafted by Lord Justice Woolf, are to be found in a 370-page document entitled "access to justice".

In the same warning bulletin, WF&D points out that it would be surprising if the liabilities of vehicle owners in the Channel Tunnel were not re-examined in the wake of last year's fire. It appears unlikely that any liability will fall on the insurers of the lorry involved, but WF&D warns that motor insurers should take note of the astronomic costs of the disaster.
It would not be difficult to envisage a similar situation in another tunnel where a lorry was being driven rather than transported, and whose owner could therefore be held liable.
